title: MCP authorization explained
heading: How Claude signs in to an MCP server
lead: A remote MCP server guards something useful, such as your tickets, documents or repositories, and will not hand it to just any program. When Claude Code connects, the server refuses the first request and points at where its sign-in rules are published. Claude then walks the OAuth 2.1 path: discover the authorization server, send you to a browser to approve, trade the resulting code for a token, and retry with that token attached. This explainer follows every request on that path and what each version of the specification changed.

facts.text: Claude Code, the MCP client; it keeps one connection and one set of tokens per server
the MCP server; it guards the tools and data and checks every token
issues the tokens; run by the server's owner or by a separate identity provider
proof that the program redeeming the code is the one that started the sign-in; mandatory in OAuth 2.1
Claude never sees your password. It sees a short-lived token that works for one server only

versions.label: Mar '25
versions.note: Authorization enters the spec: OAuth 2.1 with PKCE, metadata discovery and dynamic client registration. The MCP server is both the resource and the authorization server.

versions.label: Jun '25
versions.note: The MCP server becomes a plain resource server: protected resource metadata points at the authorization server, and tokens are bound to one server with resource indicators.

versions.label: Nov '25
versions.note: Client ID metadata documents join dynamic registration as a way to identify a client, and a server can ask for more scope step by step.

body: Claude does not know in advance whether a server wants a token. It simply sends the first MCP request, `initialize`, and lets the server answer. A server that requires authorization replies **401 Unauthorized** with a `WWW-Authenticate` header, the standard HTTP way of saying "you need credentials, and here is what kind".

Since the June 2025 revision the header also carries a `resource_metadata` URL. That one pointer removes all configuration: Claude fetches the document, learns which authorization server protects this MCP server and what scopes exist, and can start the sign-in without anyone typing a URL.

versionNotes.heading: In 2025-03-26
items: A bare 401. The client assumes the MCP server is also the authorization server and looks for metadata at the server's own origin.
The 401 carries `resource_metadata`, a URL to the protected resource metadata document (RFC 9728).
The MCP server is a resource server only; the authorization server may be anyone.

steps.title: Try without a token
steps.explanation: You add the server; Claude opens its MCP endpoint and sends the first request of any session. There is no token yet, so the server refuses and says where its sign-in rules are published.

messages.name: add server mcp.example.com
messages.info: connect to a remote MCP server

annotations.text: The Streamable HTTP transport lets the server answer with plain JSON or with an event stream; the client accepts both.
`initialize` always goes first. The server has not seen a token, so it never gets to run it.
The scheme is `Bearer`: present a token in the Authorization header. The parameter says where to learn how to get one.
URL of the protected resource metadata (RFC 9728). Claude fetches it next; nothing about the server is configured by hand.
In the first revision the header carried no pointer. The client assumed the MCP server itself issues tokens and looked for metadata at its origin.

steps.title: Read the protected resource metadata
steps.explanation: Claude fetches the document the 401 pointed at. It names the authorization servers that protect this resource and the scopes the server understands.

check.prompt: Where does Claude learn which authorization server to talk to?

options.text: From the metadata document the 401 pointed at
options.why: Right. The server publishes it at a well-known path and names its authorization servers there, so no client needs a list of servers built in.

options.text: From a list of known authorization servers shipped with Claude
options.why: A built-in list would break for every new server. The protocol makes the server announce its own authorization server.

options.text: By asking you to type the sign-in URL
options.why: You never type anything but your password, and you type that into the authorization server's own page, not into Claude.

annotations.text: The identifier of this protected resource. Claude will ask for tokens bound to exactly this value.
Who issues tokens for it. One is usual; with several, the client picks one it can work with.
`header` only: the token travels in the Authorization header, never in the URL.

2025-03-26.title: Assume the server issues its own tokens
2025-03-26.explanation: The first revision had no protected resource metadata. Claude assumed the MCP server was also the authorization server and went straight to its origin for the authorization server metadata.

messages.name: authorization server = https://mcp.example.com
messages.info: derived from the MCP endpoint's origin

body: An OAuth authorization server describes itself in a JSON document at a well-known path (RFC 8414). It lists the endpoints a client needs, the code challenge methods it accepts and the ways a client may register. Claude fetches it once per server and caches it.

Two details matter for MCP. The server **must** support PKCE with `S256`; a client refuses to continue without it. And the metadata may name a registration endpoint, which decides how Claude will identify itself in the next topic.

steps.title: Fetch the authorization server metadata
steps.explanation: Claude takes the authorization server's URL and asks for its well-known metadata. OpenID-style discovery at a different path is tried as a fallback.

annotations.text: The server's identity. Claude keys stored tokens by it, so two servers behind different issuers never mix.
Must include `S256`. Without PKCE an intercepted code could be redeemed by someone else.
Present when the server accepts dynamic client registration; optional.
`none` means a public client like Claude, which cannot keep a secret, may use the token endpoint with PKCE alone.

steps.title: Check the essentials
steps.explanation: Before anything leaves the machine, Claude checks that the metadata supports the authorization code grant with PKCE S256 and notes the endpoints it will use.

messages.name: verify metadata
messages.payload:
response_types_supported     includes "code"        ok
code_challenge_methods       includes "S256"        ok
authorization_endpoint       https://auth.example.com/authorize
token_endpoint               https://auth.example.com/token
registration_endpoint        https://auth.example.com/register   (optional)

topics.title: Identify the client
topics.subtitle: Dynamic registration or a metadata document

body: OAuth was designed for apps that register with a service by hand and receive a `client_id`. MCP clients connect to servers nobody registered them with, so the spec needs a way for a client to introduce itself on the fly. The first answer was **dynamic client registration** (RFC 7591): post a description, receive a `client_id`.

The November 2025 revision added **client ID metadata documents**: the `client_id` is itself an `https` URL under the client publisher's control, and the authorization server fetches the client's description from it. No registration call, no per-server state, and the server can see who publishes the client.
Claude keeps whichever `client_id` it ended up with, per authorization server, next to the tokens.

items: Client ID metadata documents: the `client_id` is an `https` URL the authorization server dereferences for the client's metadata.
Dynamic registration remains available; a client may offer both.

steps.title: Register dynamically
steps.explanation: If the metadata lists a registration endpoint, Claude posts a short description of itself and receives a client id for this authorization server. Public clients get no secret.

messages.name: POST /register
messages.info: client name, redirect URIs, no secret

annotations.text: A loopback address on your machine. The browser will be sent back here with the code; only a program on this machine can receive it.
`none`: a desktop client cannot hide a secret, so it authenticates the code exchange with PKCE instead.
Meaningful only to this authorization server. Claude stores it next to the tokens, keyed by issuer.

steps.title: Or present a client ID metadata document
steps.explanation: Instead of registering, Claude can use an https URL as its client id. The authorization server fetches the document behind it, finds the client's name and redirect URIs, and treats the publisher of that URL as the party to trust.

messages.name: client_id = https://client.example/.well-known/oauth-client
messages.info: an https URL under the publisher's control

messages.name: GET client_id URL
messages.info: fetch and validate the client metadata document

annotations.text: Must equal the URL the document was fetched from. The server trusts the domain owner to describe their own client.
The server only redirects to URIs listed here, so a document published by the real client publisher protects its users.

2025-03-26.title: Not yet specified
2025-03-26.explanation: Client ID metadata documents arrive in the 2025-11-25 revision. In this revision a client registers dynamically or has a pre-configured client id.

2025-06-18.title: Not yet specified
2025-06-18.explanation: Client ID metadata documents arrive in the 2025-11-25 revision. In this revision a client registers dynamically or has a pre-configured client id.

body: Claude never asks for your password. It opens the authorization server's page in your browser, you sign in there, and the server sends the browser back to Claude with a one-time **authorization code**. The code is useless on its own: whoever redeems it must also present the **code verifier**, a random secret Claude generated before opening the browser and only ever sends over the back channel. The browser carried only its hash, the code challenge.
From the June 2025 revision the request also names the **resource** the token is for, so the authorization server can mint a token that works at that MCP server and nowhere else.

items: The authorization request carries `resource=` with the MCP server's URL (RFC 8707), so the token is audience-bound.

steps.title: Make a PKCE pair
steps.explanation: Claude draws a long random string, the code verifier, and hashes it into the code challenge. Only the challenge will leave the machine through the browser; the verifier stays until the token request.

messages.name: generate code_verifier and code_challenge
messages.payload:
code_verifier   = 43–128 chars from [A-Z a-z 0-9 - . _ ~], kept secret
code_challenge  = BASE64URL( SHA-256( code_verifier ) )
state           = random, to match the callback to this request

steps.title: Open the browser
steps.explanation: Claude starts a tiny web server on a loopback port to catch the callback, then opens the authorization URL in your default browser.

messages.name: open /authorize?…
messages.info: code challenge, redirect to localhost, resource

annotations.text: The hash of the verifier. Seeing it in the browser history tells an attacker nothing useful.
The MCP server's identifier from its metadata. Asks for a token whose audience is that server only.
A loopback address: only a program on your machine can receive the callback.
Random value echoed back by the server so Claude can match the callback to its own request.
Not present in this revision: tokens were not yet bound to one MCP server.

steps.title: You approve
steps.explanation: The browser shows the authorization server's own sign-in and consent page. You prove who you are to the server, never to Claude, and approve what the client may do.

messages.name: sign in, approve
messages.info: password, passkey or SSO; then consent

steps.title: Back to Claude with a code
steps.explanation: The server redirects the browser to the loopback address with a one-time code. Claude's tiny server receives it, checks the state, and closes the tab.

check.prompt: The authorization code travels through the browser and its history. Why can someone who copies it not use it?

options.text: Redeeming it requires the code verifier, which only Claude holds and never sent through the browser
options.why: Right. The token endpoint hashes the verifier and compares it to the challenge sent at the start; a thief has the code but not the verifier.

options.text: The code is encrypted with the browser's key
options.why: The code is an opaque string in a URL; nothing encrypts it. PKCE makes it worthless on its own instead.

options.text: The server only accepts it from the same IP address
options.why: IP checks would break on mobile networks and VPNs, and they are not part of OAuth. The verifier is the proof.

annotations.text: Single use and short-lived, typically under a minute. Useless without the code verifier.

messages.name: GET /callback?code=…&state=…
messages.info: to the loopback server Claude started

messages.name: check state
messages.info: must equal the state sent in step 2

topics.title: Trade the code for a token
topics.subtitle: Back channel, with proof

body: The code exchange happens directly between Claude and the authorization server, with no browser in between. Claude sends the code, the redirect URI it used, its client id, the **code verifier** and, since June 2025, the **resource**. The server hashes the verifier, compares it with the challenge it saw when the sign-in started, and only then issues tokens.

The **access token** is a bearer token: whoever presents it is served. That is why it is short-lived, scoped and bound to one audience. The **refresh token** lets Claude get a new access token later without bothering you again.

steps.title: POST to the token endpoint
steps.explanation: Claude redeems the code over HTTPS, proving it started the flow by including the code verifier.

messages.name: POST /token
messages.payload:
POST /token HTTP/1.1
Host: auth.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=authorization_code
&code=SplxlOBeZQQYbYS6WxSbIA
&redirect_uri=http://localhost:52341/callback
&client_id=cid_8f2a…
&code_verifier=dBjftJeZ4CVP-mB92K27uhbUJU1p1r_wW1gFWFOEjXk
&resource=https://mcp.example.com/mcp

annotations.text: The secret from step 1 of the sign-in. The server checks BASE64URL(SHA-256(verifier)) equals the code_challenge it stored.
Repeated here so the issued token is bound to this MCP server.
No client secret: a public client authenticates with PKCE alone.

messages.name: POST /token
messages.payload:
POST /token HTTP/1.1
Host: mcp.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=authorization_code
&code=SplxlOBeZQQYbYS6WxSbIA
&redirect_uri=http://localhost:52341/callback
&client_id=cid_8f2a…
&code_verifier=dBjftJeZ4CVP-mB92K27uhbUJU1p1r_wW1gFWFOEjXk

steps.title: Receive the tokens
steps.explanation: The server answers with a short-lived access token, its lifetime, the granted scope and a refresh token.

annotations.text: Opaque to Claude. The MCP server knows how to validate it, by signature or by asking the issuer. Its audience is the MCP server named in `resource`.
Seconds until the access token dies. Short lifetimes limit the damage of a leak.
Lets Claude get a new access token without a browser. It is the more valuable secret and is stored in the keychain.

steps.title: Store them safely
steps.explanation: Claude saves the tokens in the operating system's credential store, keyed by the authorization server and the MCP server, and never writes them to a project file.

messages.name: store credentials
messages.info: OS keychain, keyed by issuer and server
messages.payload:
keychain entry
  issuer         https://auth.example.com
  resource       https://mcp.example.com/mcp
  client_id      cid_8f2a…
  access_token   at_…        expires 2025-11-25T10:42Z
  refresh_token  rt_…

body: With a token in hand, Claude repeats the very first request, this time with an `Authorization: Bearer` header. The MCP server validates the token, in particular that its **audience** is this server, and the normal MCP session begins: initialize, list tools, call tools.

When the access token expires the server answers 401 again; Claude uses the refresh token and retries without opening a browser. When a tool needs more than the granted scope, a server following the November 2025 revision can answer **403** with `insufficient_scope` and the scope it wants; Claude then runs the sign-in again asking for the union of old and new scopes.

items: Scope challenges: a 403 with `insufficient_scope` names the scope a request needs, and the client asks for it incrementally.

steps.title: Retry the first request
steps.explanation: The same initialize request, now with the bearer token. The server checks signature, expiry and audience, then answers as any MCP server would.

messages.name: POST /mcp
messages.payload:
POST /mcp HTTP/1.1
Host: mcp.example.com
Authorization: Bearer at_2YotnFZFEjr1zCsicMWpAA…
Content-Type: application/json

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-11-25","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"claude-code","version":"2.x"}}}

annotations.text: The bearer token, in the header only. Never in the URL, never in the JSON body.

messages.name: validate token
messages.payload:
signature   issuer's key           ok
expiry      not before now         ok
audience    https://mcp.example.com/mcp   ok   (reject anything else)
scope       mcp:tools mcp:resources

steps.title: Refresh when it expires
steps.explanation: An hour later the access token is dead. The server says 401, Claude posts the refresh token to the token endpoint and continues. You notice nothing.

messages.name: 401 Unauthorized
messages.payload:
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token", error_description="The access token expired"

messages.name: 200 OK
messages.info: new access token, maybe a new refresh token

annotations.text: Many servers rotate it on every use; Claude replaces the stored one and the old one stops working.

messages.name: POST /mcp
messages.info: the failed request, retried with the new token

steps.title: Step up for more scope
steps.explanation: A tool needs a scope the token does not carry. The server refuses with 403 and names the missing scope; Claude asks for the union of the old and new scopes and repeats the browser sign-in.

messages.name: 403 Forbidden
messages.payload:
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="insufficient_scope", scope="tickets:write", resource_metadata="https://mcp.example.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource"

annotations.text: What this request needs. The client asks for the union of what it has and what is missing, so it does not lose the old grant.

messages.name: open /authorize?…&scope=… tickets:write
messages.info: the sign-in again, with more scope

2025-03-26.title: No step-up path
2025-03-26.explanation: Scope challenges arrive in the 2025-11-25 revision. Earlier, a client that lacked a scope could only start a fresh sign-in on its own initiative.

2025-06-18.explanation: Scope challenges arrive in the 2025-11-25 revision. Earlier, a client that lacked a scope could only start a fresh sign-in on its own initiative.

body: Many MCP servers are thin wrappers around another API. The tempting shortcut is to take the token Claude sent and forward it upstream. The spec forbids it: the token's audience is the MCP server, not the upstream API, and an upstream that accepts it cannot tell whether the request was authorised for this purpose. A server that forwards tokens becomes a **confused deputy**, lending its authority to whoever can reach it.

The right design is two tokens: Claude's token proves the user to the MCP server, and the MCP server obtains its own credentials for the upstream, by token exchange, by its own client credentials, or by a separate consent for the upstream. Each token means one thing to one audience.

items: Token passthrough is explicitly forbidden; servers must validate that a token was issued for them.
A security best practices document accompanies the authorization spec.

items.text: A token has one audience. If you did not mint or request it for the service you are calling, do not send it there.

steps.title: The tempting shortcut
steps.explanation: The MCP server receives a tool call with Claude's bearer token and simply forwards that token to the upstream API. The upstream either rejects it for the wrong audience or, worse, accepts it without knowing who approved what.

check.prompt: The MCP server must call a third-party API on your behalf. What may it do with the token Claude sent?

options.text: Validate it for its own use and obtain its own token for the upstream
options.why: Right. Claude's token proves the user to the MCP server only. The server gets separate credentials for the upstream, so every token has exactly one audience.

options.text: Forward it as it is, since you already consented
options.why: You consented to the MCP server, not to every service it talks to. Forwarding makes the server a confused deputy and is forbidden by the spec.

options.text: Forward it after checking that its scope covers the API
options.why: Scope is not audience. Even a token with a matching scope was minted for the MCP server, and the upstream cannot tell how the request was authorised.

messages.name: GET /repos
messages.payload:
GET /repos HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.net
Authorization: Bearer at_2YotnFZFEjr1zCsicMWpAA…   <- minted for mcp.example.com, not for api.example.net

annotations.text: The wrong token for this audience. An upstream that checks audiences rejects it; one that does not has just been fooled.

steps.title: The right way
steps.explanation: The MCP server validates Claude's token for itself, then gets its own token for the upstream, here by exchanging the user's token at the authorization server, and calls the upstream with that.

annotations.text: The server asks for a token that is valid at the upstream and says so. The authorization server decides whether this delegation is allowed.

body: A bearer token is only as safe as the set of places that accept it. If one token worked at every MCP server behind the same authorization server, a rogue server you were tricked into connecting to could take the token you sent it and replay it at the real one. **Resource indicators** (RFC 8707) close that hole: the client names the server it wants a token for, the authorization server records that audience in the token, and every server rejects tokens whose audience is not itself.
This is why the June 2025 revision made the `resource` parameter mandatory in both the authorization and the token request, and why servers must check it.

items: `resource` is required in the authorization and token requests; tokens carry an audience and servers must check it.

steps.title: A token minted for one server
steps.explanation: Because Claude named the resource when it asked, the token it holds carries that server as its audience.

steps.title: Replayed at another server
steps.explanation: Suppose you were tricked into connecting Claude to a rogue server and it received a token. It tries to use that token at the real server. The audience check stops it.

messages.name: POST /mcp
messages.info: a token minted for evil.example, not for mcp.example.com

messages.name: validate token
messages.payload:
audience   https://evil.example/mcp
expected   https://mcp.example.com/mcp
result     REJECT

footer: Written from the MCP specification revisions 2025-03-26, 2025-06-18 and 2025-11-25 and the OAuth RFCs they cite. Hostnames, ports, ids and tokens are illustrative. Claude Code is one MCP client; any compliant client follows the same path.
